q: What are Romanesque walls typically like?
n: Romanesque walls are massive and thick, needed to carry the heavy stone barrel and groin vaults with few openings. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What arch is typical of Romanesque architecture?
n: Romanesque architecture uses the semicircular (round) arch inherited from Roman building. The pointed arch is Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Romanesque architecture.

q: What buttress is typical of Romanesque buildings?
n: Romanesque buttresses are flat pilaster strips (lesenes) of small projection set against thick walls. Flying buttresses are a Gothic development. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What are Romanesque windows typically like?
n: Romanesque windows are few and small, because large openings would weaken the thick load-bearing walls that resist the vault thrust. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Romanesque cathedrals generally follow which plan?
n: Romanesque churches follow the basilican Latin-cross plan: a long nave crossed by transepts, with an apse and often an ambulatory and radiating chapels. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the most spectacular Byzantine church, begun in AD 532?
n: Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (532–537), by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus for Emperor Justinian, is the supreme Byzantine church. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is Byzantium, capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, called today?
n: Byzantium was refounded as Constantinople in 330 and is today Istanbul, Turkey. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Istanbul.

q: What is the distinctive form of a Byzantine church?
o: Greek cross plan with a dome
n: The typical Byzantine church is centrally planned on a Greek cross, crowned by a dome on pendentives. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Byzantine architecture.

q: Which was the first church built in Constantinople and defined by its large atrium?
n: Hagia Irene is traditionally the first church built in Constantinople, commissioned by Constantine I in the 4th century and rebuilt by Justinian. It keeps its large atrium. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Irene; Istanbul museums (Hagia Irene).

q: What spherical triangle, perfected by Byzantine builders, carries a dome over a square?
n: A pendentive is a concave spherical triangle that carries a circular dome over a square bay, perfected by Byzantine builders at Hagia Sophia. A squinch does the same job with an arch across the corner. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the Leaning Tower of Pisa called in Italian?
n: In Italian the Leaning Tower of Pisa is the "Torre pendente di Pisa" ("pendente" means leaning). Source: Opera della Primaziale Pisana (official site).

q: Who is traditionally credited as architect of the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
n: Bonanno Pisano is traditionally credited as the first architect of the Leaning Tower (begun 1173), though scholars also propose Diotisalvi or Gherardo di Gherardo. Source: Opera della Primaziale Pisana; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is the architectural style of the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
n: The Leaning Tower is a campanile in the Pisan (Italian) Romanesque style, with tiers of arcades like the cathedral beside it. Source: UNESCO (Piazza del Duomo, Pisa).

q: When was construction of the Leaning Tower of Pisa completed?
n: The tower was built in three stages from 1173. The bell chamber, completed by Tommaso Pisano, was finished in 1372. Source: Opera della Primaziale Pisana; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is the height of the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
n: The Leaning Tower is about 55.86 m (183.3 ft) tall on its low side and about 56.67 m on its high side. 183.33 ft is the commonly cited figure. Source: Opera della Primaziale Pisana; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Characteristic of a Gothic bell tower?
n: Gothic bell towers and west-front towers are tall, often topped with spires, reinforcing the vertical emphasis of the style. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the usual shape of a Gothic arch?
n: The Gothic arch is pointed. Its steeper shape directs thrust more nearly downward and allows bays of varying width to rise to the same height. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: What is a Gothic church interior like?
n: Gothic interiors are tall, light and airy. Ribbed vaults and flying buttresses free the walls for large stained-glass windows. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: What buttress is typical of Gothic architecture?
n: The flying buttress, an arch carrying vault thrust across the aisles to an outer pier, is the signature Gothic support. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: When did Gothic architecture flourish?
n: Gothic architecture began with Abbot Suger's choir at Saint-Denis about 1140 and flourished until the 15th–16th centuries. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: What carries the dome in a Byzantine church?
n: In a Byzantine church the dome sits on pendentives, which bring the square of four piers and arches to the dome's circular base. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher.

q: Which was the first church built in Constantinople, by Emperor Constantine I?
n: Hagia Irene is considered the first church built in Constantinople, commissioned by Constantine I before Hagia Sophia. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Irene.

q: The original exterior color of this church was white. In present day, its exterior developed to a colorful one.
n: St. Basil's Cathedral in Moscow (1555–61) was originally white with golden domes, matching the Kremlin. Its famous multicoloured onion domes and painted surfaces were added mainly in the 17th–19th centuries. Source: State Historical Museum, Moscow (St. Basil's Cathedral); UNESCO (Kremlin and Red Square).

q: Which is characteristic of Byzantine architecture?
n: Byzantine churches are typically centrally planned on a Greek cross (cross-in-square), with a dome on pendentives over the crossing. Flying buttresses are Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Byzantine architecture.

q: Byzantine architecture had its golden age under Justinian, between:
n: Byzantine architecture reached its first golden age under Emperor Justinian I, who reigned AD 527–565. Hagia Sophia, San Vitale and Hagia Irene's rebuilding date from his reign. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Justinian I.

q: Which style is marked by tall pointed arches?
n: Tall pointed arches, with rib vaults and flying buttresses, are the defining marks of Gothic architecture. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which style brought back classical elements?
n: The Renaissance (from about 1420 in Florence) revived classical Greek and Roman orders, proportion and symmetry. Brunelleschi and Alberti led the way. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Renaissance architecture; Fletcher.

q: Whatarchitectural style is characterized by ornamented arcades, walls, windows, and arches?
n: Romanesque buildings are marked by round-arched arcades, including blind arcades and arcaded galleries, on walls, windows and portals, as at Pisa and Lucca. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Romanesque architecture.

q: Which style uses rock-like forms and scalloped shells for a lavish effect?
n: Rococo takes its name from rocaille, rock-like and shell-like ornament. It is a lighter, playful, asymmetrical development of late Baroque. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Rococo.

q: Which style is marked by rich, exuberant, full ornament?
n: Baroque architecture (17th century) is rich and theatrical: curving facades, dramatic light and abundant sculptural ornament. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Baroque architecture.

q: Which French Gothic cathedral has the loftiest vault?
n: Beauvais Cathedral has the tallest Gothic choir vault ever built, about 48 m. It partly collapsed in 1284 and had to be rebuilt with extra piers. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Beauvais Cathedral.

q: Which church is known as a famous pilgrimage site?
n: Chartres Cathedral has been a major Marian pilgrimage site since the Middle Ages. It houses the Sancta Camisa, the tunic said to be the Virgin Mary's. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral).

q: Which cathedral is famous for its stained-glass rose windows?
n: Chartres Cathedral keeps the most complete set of medieval stained glass in the world, including its three great rose windows. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral).

q: Which French Gothic cathedral was never finished after structural collapses?
n: Beauvais Cathedral was never completed. Its choir vault fell in 1284 and its crossing tower collapsed in 1573, and no nave was ever built. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Beauvais Cathedral.

q: Which Gothic cathedral was the coronation site of French kings?
n: Reims Cathedral was the traditional coronation church of the kings of France. Source: UNESCO (Cathedral of Notre-Dame, Reims).
